newsitem.title: USA: Access Health falls on revised outlook.
newsitem.headline: Access Health falls on revised outlook.

text.p: Shares of personal health management services provider Access Health Inc fell sharply on the company's prediction that fiscal 1997 earnings would be as much as 17 percent under analyst estimates.

Access, which contracts to employers and health care providers, cited slower enrollment growth and competitive pricing as its customers grew more cautious about the cost savings potential of its services.
But Access reiterated Wednesday it was confident sales and earnings next year would grow by at least 35 percent.
"We are still showing a very strong growth rate and we feel we are being conservative today saying we see 35 percent growth in 1998," Matt Plavan, director of investor relations told Reuters.
Plavan said much of the growth potential came from new customers in the health plans Access currently services.
"If you think about the fact we have 21 million members out of the 60 million members in the plans we currently serve, there is great opportunity to expand beyond 21 million (members)," he said.

Although Access contracts with a large number of health care providers, many of those customers are under pressure to control their own costs and have purchased Access services for only a portion of their customers as a way to test the cost benefits.

"This is a transition year for large health care plans," Plavan said. "More of them are saying to us, 'Can you show me the return on our investment?'" He said health plans were more focused two years ago on retaining customers by providing superior services.

Access services include health information, prevention and care management programs that are available over the internet, on cable television, and through 24-hour telephone access to registered nurses who provide triage and referral services.

Plavan said Access believes its services are one of the best ways for health plans to control their own costs since its network is broader than what most individual health plans could reasonably offer on their own.
However, some analysts cited concerns that more health plans will follow the decision by BlueCross Blue Shield of Tennessee to drop the service and have its own doctors perform triage work.

"Right now, that decision seems to be specific to Tennessee," said Equitable Securities analyst Seth Frank. "At the same time, there is certainly reason to be a little bit cautious about other health plans."
